title: Who won, and who went first
lede: Blockbuster outlived the chains it had beaten. [Hollywood Video](/hollywood-video/) and Movie Gallery were liquidated months before Blockbuster filed. The businesses that replaced all three did not rent from a shop.

blocks.title: Five ways to rent a film. One is still growing.
blocks.subtitle: The video rental field, and what became of each.

items.name: Blockbuster
items.text: At the 2004 peak. Chapter 11 in 2010, sold to Dish in 2011, one franchise left.[^6][^11][^13][^31]

items.name: Netflix
items.text: Revenue in 2025. It had 857,000 subscribers at the end of 2002 and 20 million at the end of 2010.[^23][^21][^22]

items.name: Redbox
items.text: At the end of 2010, with $1.16B of revenue. Shut down in July 2024 when its last owner’s bankruptcy became a liquidation.[^24][^34]

items.name: Hollywood Video
items.text: Price Movie Gallery paid in 2005, after Blockbuster let its own $14.50 a share offer lapse. Liquidated with its parent in 2010.[^26][^5]

items.name: Movie Gallery
items.text: After buying Hollywood. It entered bankruptcy in October 2007 and moved to close its last 1,900-plus stores in May 2010.[^25][^26]

blocks.source: Company filings and press as cited. Sparklines: Blockbuster year-end stores[^2][^6][^8][^9][^10]; Netflix annual revenue 2002–2010[^21][^22]; Redbox (Coinstar DVD Services) revenue 2008–2010[^24].

blocks.note: Year labels are fiscal years. Blockbuster’s points for 2007 to 2010 are January 6, 2008, January 4, 2009, January 3, 2010 and January 2, 2011, and its counts exclude kiosks. Hollywood Video’s counts exclude its Game Crazy departments, and its series stops with its FY2004 10-K; that says nothing about later filings. Movie Gallery’s 2004 point is January 2, 2005. Its 2005 total includes Hollywood Video, which it bought that year, so the step from 2004 to 2005 is an acquisition, not growth. Its 2007 point is the company’s own figure of approximately 3,900 at January 6, 2008. The three scopes differ, so read the lines as trends, not as a ranking.

blocks.title: Netflix subscribers against Blockbuster Online
blocks.subtitle: Millions of subscribers at year end. Blockbuster reported its online count only for the years shown.
blocks.source: Netflix FY2006 and FY2010 10-Ks[^21][^22]. Blockbuster: about 1.2 million at December 31, 2005 and about 2.2 million at December 31, 2006[^6][^7]. Blockbuster also reported more than 750,000 on March 9, 2005[^5].

blocks.body: Blockbuster tried to buy Hollywood Entertainment in early 2005, offering $11.50 in cash and $3.00 in stock per share. It let the offer expire on March 24, 2005, citing “the unlikely resolution of the Company’s request for regulatory clearance on an acceptable timetable.”[^5]

Hollywood Entertainment, the chain Blockbuster bid for, was profitable when the offer lapsed. Its FY2004 10-K reports restated net income of $71.3M on revenue of $1.78B for 2004, and long-term obligations, including the current portion, of $351.3M at the end of that year.[^44] Blockbuster’s own 2004 result is in The numbers.
